title: Partial charges explain dipole and ion-dipole strength
body: Judge the strength and orientation dependence of dipole-dipole and ion-dipole forces by the sign of the partial charges behind the molecular dipole moment and how those charges interact with an ion or an adjacent dipole.
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.3: "considering the sign of the partial charges responsible for the molecular dipole moment, and how these partial charges interact with an ion or with an adjacent dipole"

title: Polar vs. nonpolar molecules of similar size
body: Interactions between polar molecules are typically greater than those between nonpolar molecules of comparable size, because dipole-dipole interactions act in addition to London dispersion forces.
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.2: "Interactions between polar molecules are typically greater than those between nonpolar molecules of comparable size because these interactions act in addition to London dispersion forces."

title: Dipole-dipole interactions
body: Dipole-dipole interactions are attractions present between polar molecules, and their strength depends on the magnitudes of the dipoles and their relative orientation.
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.2: "Dipole-dipole interactions are present between polar molecules. The interaction strength depends on the magnitudes of the dipoles and their relative orientation."

title: Hydrogen bonding
body: Hydrogen bonding is a strong type of intermolecular interaction in which a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to N, O, or F is attracted to the negative end of a dipole formed by N, O, or F in a different molecule, or a different part of the same molecule.
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.4: "Hydrogen bonding is a strong type of intermolecular interaction that exists when hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to the highly electronegative atoms (N, O, and F) are attracted to the negative end of a dipole"

title: Noncovalent interactions in large biomolecules
body: In large biomolecules and polymers, noncovalent interactions can occur between different molecules or between different regions of the same molecule, and they largely dictate the molecule's shape, functionality, and properties.
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.5 and 3.2.A.7: "noncovalent interactions may occur between different molecules or between different regions of the same large biomolecule"

title: Particulate model of solid, liquid, and gas
body: A particulate-level model shows how particle arrangement, spacing, and motion differ among the solid, liquid, and gas phases.

items.label: Solid (crystalline or amorphous)
items.meaning: Particles are in close contact. They are in a regular 3-D arrangement if crystalline and an irregular one if amorphous. Motion is limited, with no overall translation of particles relative to each other.

items.label: Liquid
items.meaning: Particles are in close contact, similar in molar volume to the solid, and are continually moving and colliding. Their arrangement and movement depend on the nature and strength of the forces between them.

items.label: Gas
items.meaning: Particles are in constant motion with minimal effects from forces between them. Collision frequency and average spacing depend on temperature, pressure, and volume. The gas has neither a definite volume nor a definite shape.

ced_evidence: 3.3.A.1-3.3.A.4: "Represent the differences between solid, liquid, and gas phases using a particulate-level model"

title: Causes of deviation from ideal gas behavior
body: Real gases can deviate from the ideal gas law for two reasons named in the CED.

items.label: Interparticle attractions
items.meaning: Attractions among gas molecules, particularly at conditions close to those resulting in condensation.

items.label: Particle volumes
items.meaning: The volume of the particles themselves, particularly at extremely high pressures.

ced_evidence: 3.6.A.1: "Deviations from the ideal gas law may result from interparticle attractions among gas molecules... Deviations may also arise from particle volumes"

title: Chromatography
body: Chromatography (paper, thin-layer, and column) separates chemical species by the differential strength of intermolecular interactions between the components of the mobile phase and the surface components of the stationary phase, and the resulting chromatogram can be used to infer the relative polarities of the components.
ced_evidence: 3.9.A.1: "Chromatography (paper, thin-layer, and column) separates chemical species by taking advantage of the differential strength of intermolecular interactions"

title: Particulate representation of a solution
body: A particulate model of a solution communicates its structure and properties by showing the interactions among components and the relative concentrations of components.

items.label: Interactions between components
items.meaning: Drawings that show the interactions among the solute and solvent components.

items.label: Concentrations of components
items.meaning: The relative numbers of particles of each component in the solution.

ced_evidence: 3.8.A.1: "Particulate representations of solutions communicate the structure and properties of solutions, by illustration of the relative concentrations of the components in the solution and/or drawings that show interactions among the components."
